# Implement block: Exertion Spectrum Slider (SwiftUI)

You are adding the "Exertion Spectrum Slider" block from Native Cook to the user's iOS app. The block already exists as working SwiftUI code. Your job is to bring it into this project faithfully, not to write a new one that looks similar.

## The block

A dark rating sheet with rounded top corners over a page whose blurred traces show through: "How hard was it?" and a grey subtitle, one huge white numeral from 1 to 10 (112 pt bold), the level's name ("Very Light") and one or two grey lines describing it, then a slider, "Clear Entry", "How to Self-Assess" and a full-width Save button. The slider's track is a 9 pt line filled with a spectrum (teal, sky blue, yellow, orange, red, magenta, purple) with a dot between levels, lit from the usual range to the thumb and shaded beyond; a band of grey diagonal hatching marks everything outside the "USUAL RANGE", and the thumb is a white disc with a dot in the colour under it. Touching the slider swells the track into a wedge, 9 pt at the left and 54 pt at the right, and fills the thumb with its colour; dragging rolls the numeral like a counter wheel with a vertical blur at every level, cross-fades the name and description, and runs Save's fill along the spectrum. Outside the usual range the hatching between the range and the thumb takes the spectrum's colours, a red "ABOVE USUAL RANGE" or cyan "BELOW USUAL RANGE" tag pops in over the thumb in place of the caption, and Save gains a second line; letting go shrinks the track back, and "Clear Entry" sends the thumb home.

**Motion.** The track is cut into as many equal parts as there are levels; the level is the part the thumb is in, and a level's own colour is the spectrum at the middle of its part. The thumb never jumps: it follows the finger's place on a spring (mass 1, stiffness 520, damping 44), keeping its offset when it was caught within 28 pt and coming to the finger when the track was touched elsewhere; it is not snapped on release. Touch-down sets a swell that a spring carries from 0 to 1 (stiffness 300, damping 21, a slight overshoot): the track's outline is blended between the 9 pt line and the wedge (9 pt at the left, 54 pt at the right, 5 pt corners), the dots between levels grow into lines 34% of the track's thickness, the thumb grows from 28 to 30 pt and its dot from 11 to 24 pt, and the lit hatching goes from 45% to full strength; release runs it back. At every change of level the numeral rolls for 240 ms with a cubic ease-out: digits sit 86 pt apart on a vertical strip, a higher level coming up from below, each fading with its distance from the centre (gone one step away) while the strip is blurred by sin(pi x progress) x 13 pt along the roll and 2.5 pt across; a new change retargets the roll from where it is. The name and description cross-fade in 160 ms, Save's fill travels along the levels' colours for 260 ms (linear), and a selection haptic ticks. The spectrum is shaded by 46% black left of min(thumb, range start) and right of max(thumb, range end). Leaving the usual range pops the tag over the thumb (scale 0.7 to 1 and 6 pt up, spring stiffness 420, damping 22; it follows the thumb, kept 12 pt inside the screen), fades the caption out and Save's second line in over 200 ms while its label moves up 8 pt, and draws a white needle through the thumb; coming back reverses it. "Clear Entry" (dim and disabled at the opening level) puts the thumb's target back, so the numeral rolls through the levels in between. The self-playing demo, period 9.4 s: touch at 0.8 s, drag from level 2 to 8 between 1.15 and 4.25 s (55% linear plus 45% smoothstep), hold, back to level 4 between 4.7 and 6.2 s, lift at 6.6 s, Clear Entry pressed at 7.4 s for 150 ms; it gives no haptics, and a touch stops it until 3 s after the last one, when the thumb goes home and the loop starts again 0.8 s later. Under reduced motion the springs jump (the track swaps between line and wedge, the thumb moves at once), the numeral cross-fades in place with no blur, and the tags fade. The native ports clear manual haptic ownership before the automatic return home, keeping all autoPlay motion silent; React Native retains that ownership until the next loop starts and can tick during this return. SwiftUI approximates the anisotropic numeral blur with a small horizontal blur and nine weighted vertical canvas samples. Jetpack Compose uses anisotropic image blur on Android 12 and newer and dims the moving digits below that; Android 8.0–8.1 canvas shadows use weighted drawing layers instead of hardware blur masks.

## Reference source

The block is built and running in the Native Cook source repository. Each link below is a file on GitHub. To read one as plain text, replace `https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/` with `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/` in its address.

### Demo (start here)

- [ExertionSpectrumSliderDemo.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Forms/ExertionSpectrumSlider/ExertionSpectrumSliderDemo.swift)

### Files of the block

- [ExertionSpectrumSlider.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Forms/ExertionSpectrumSlider/ExertionSpectrumSlider.swift)

### Shared helpers the block uses

- [swift/NativeCook/Shared/ComponentSupport.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Shared/ComponentSupport.swift)

### Frameworks

It needs no framework beyond SwiftUI.

## Your instructions

_Anything specific to this app goes here: where the block should appear, what to rename, what to change. Left empty, integrate the block as it is._

## How to work

Work like an experienced iOS engineer joining an existing project: learn the app first, read only what you need, decide early how the block fits, then integrate it with as little disruption as possible. Take the steps in order.

**Done means** the block is reachable in the user's app and behaves like the reference in the iOS Simulator or on a device. A SwiftUI preview is useful while you work, but it is not the proof: build and run the app.

**Fidelity.** Bring over the real implementation. Keep its structure, colours, sizes, timings and curves. Change only what this project requires and what "Your instructions" ask for.

If you already learned this project earlier in the conversation, reuse what you know and skip step 2. Learn it again only if the project changed or something you need is missing.

### 1. Check where you are

- You need the project's files and a terminal. If this prompt was pasted into a chat that has neither, stop and say so: it has to be run by a coding agent opened on the project.
- Confirm the project is an iOS app built with Xcode (an `.xcodeproj`, an `.xcworkspace` or a Swift package with an app target). If it is something else, stop, say what you found, and do not create a new app inside it unless the instructions ask for one.

### 2. Learn the host app

- The app target, its deployment target and its Swift version.
- SwiftUI, UIKit or both, and how a screen is shown today: `NavigationStack`, a coordinator, a tab bar, a storyboard.
- How files join the target: a folder the project synchronises, or a file list in the project that you have to extend.
- Conventions: folder layout, naming, where colours, fonts and assets live.
- Type names the app already uses, so the block's types do not collide with them.

### 3. Read the block

- Swift files in a module do not import each other, so the demo alone will not lead you to the rest. The list above names every file of the block: read them all.
- The demo is how the source repository shows the block. Bring over what the demo shows, not the repository's gallery. Anything listed under "Used by the demo only" stays behind.
- Read the block's initialiser and its defaults. The demo may switch on an option that makes the block play by itself for a recording (for example `autoPlay`). Keep the option; leave it off in the user's app unless asked.

### 4. Decide the fit

- The source app targets iOS 17. If the host targets an older system, check each API the block uses and tell the user what would have to change before you lower anything. Do not raise the host's deployment target without asking.
- If a type or function name of the block already exists in the app, rename the block's one, in every file that uses it, and say that you did.
- Shared helpers: copy the ones the block uses next to it, or fold them into the block's files. Do not copy helpers it never calls.
- In a UIKit app, show the block through a `UIHostingController`.

### 5. Bring it in

- Add the block's files to the app target, keeping their names.
- Copy its asset catalogs, loose resources and fonts, and check that the names the code asks for match the names in the bundle: a wrong name compiles and then shows nothing.
- A `.metal` file has to be compiled into the same target as the code that calls its function.
- Keep reduced-motion handling, haptics and accessibility labels as they are in the source.
- Mount the block where the instructions say. With no instructions, add a screen named after the block and make it reachable the way the app's other screens are.

### 6. Run it

- Build the app target for a simulator with `xcodebuild` or the project's own script, and fix every error and new warning the block introduced.
- Run it and use the block: every state, every gesture, light and dark appearance if the block follows them, and once with Reduce Motion on.
- If the build or the simulator fails for a reason outside the block, report the error and ask how to continue.

### 7. Report

- Files added and changed, and anything renamed to avoid a collision.
- How to reach the block in the app.
- Anything that differs from the reference, and why.
